title: Hip fracture trauma unit: early physiotherapy and prolonged stay, conflicting evidence and a reopen after partial work
notes: Demanding path on an explicit case-control need: a physiotherapy lead wants to know whether mobilisation within 24 hours of hip fracture surgery goes with shorter stays, with exposure only in paper notes. A fixture search returns seven records that conflict: a randomised trial in selected patients finds stays 2.3 days shorter, a registry analysis finds no difference after adjustment, and a review finds heterogeneous results. The appraisal records the conflict honestly as claim c3, an inference resting on the three records with uncertainty 'high', alongside source-derived claims with exact passages; certainty is low. The decision (kind narrow) rests on c3, c4 and c5; the ethics gate is unknown, so acceptance gives an accepted selection and a blocked action. The study is reopened after the Protocol stage (eight of 13 stages): completed work, the high-uncertainty claim and the decision must be intact and the later stages incomplete. The remaining five stages are then finished, followed by reload and export. Record ids are stableRecordId values as in src/lib/evidence/records.ts at 875fe59: DOI hash for records 1, 3, 4, 5, 7 (ev-019gs0m, ev-0bu9ox0, ev-0xo0saw, ev-0go084z, ev-1p5a657); titleYearKey hash for records 2 and 6 (ev-1lrsu2p, ev-005ikon). Requires S13 (appraisal and ledger), S11 (selectionStatus, actionStatus, basis) and D5 (status text). Catches: conflicting evidence flattened into a confident claim, an uncertainty label changed on reload, partial work lost or stages wrongly marked complete on reopen, and an action allowed past an unknown gate.

inputs.need:
I am the clinical lead physiotherapist for the orthopaedic trauma unit of a 700-bed hospital, where we treat about 420 adults with hip fracture a year. The national hip fracture standard says patients should be helped out of bed by a physiotherapist on the day after surgery, but on our unit only about half are mobilised within 24 hours and the rest wait one to three days, mainly because of weekend staffing, low blood pressure after surgery or delirium. Our median length of stay is 19 days and the hospital wants it shorter.

I want to find out whether patients who were mobilised by a physiotherapist within 24 hours of surgery had shorter stays, before I ask for weekend physiotherapy cover. The difficulty is data. Physiotherapy entries before 2025 were handwritten and exist only in the paper notes, which our clerical team can pull, and working out the time of first mobilisation takes about 25 minutes per patient. We cannot read the notes of every patient treated from 2022 to 2024.

My plan is a case-control study: cases would be patients whose stay was longer than 28 days and controls patients discharged within 28 days, sampled from the unit's hip fracture list, and we would compare how many in each group were mobilised within 24 hours, taking account of age, mobility before the fracture, dementia and the type of operation. I have read papers saying that early mobilisation shortens stays and others saying it makes no difference once you allow for how unwell patients are, so I need help with confounding, how many notes we need to read and how to define the time of first mobilisation.
inputs.constraints: About 100 hours of clerical and physiotherapy time for reading notes; paper notes for 2022 to 2024 only; no contact with patients; results needed for the service planning round in April 2027.
localFacts: About 420 adults with hip fracture are treated on the unit each year; the median length of stay is 19 days.
The unit's hip fracture list gives admission, operation and discharge dates and the operation type for every patient since 2022.
The Head of Therapies approved 100 hours of note reading between November 2026 and March 2027 (memo THR-2026-12).
The hospital research ethics board has not yet reviewed the proposal.

records.title: Physiotherapist-led mobilisation within 24 hours of hip fracture surgery and length of stay: a randomised trial in two trauma units
records.authors: Brennan-Adeyemi C, Solberg-Mwangi T, Okafor-Reyes L
records.abstract: We randomised 260 adults after hip fracture surgery in two trauma units to physiotherapist-led mobilisation within 24 hours or to usual care, in which first mobilisation occurred at a median of 46 hours. Mean length of stay was 13.1 days with early mobilisation and 15.4 days with usual care (difference minus 2.3 days, 95 percent CI minus 4.0 to minus 0.6). Walking ability at 30 days was better in the early group. Patients with severe dementia, postoperative hypotension requiring treatment or delirium at the time of randomisation were excluded, about 30 percent of those screened. Both units provided physiotherapy seven days a week.

records.title: Early mobilisation and length of stay after hip fracture: a registry analysis adjusting for frailty and delirium
records.abstract: Using a national hip fracture registry, we studied 6,400 patients from 38 hospitals. Patients first mobilised within 24 hours of surgery had a median stay three days shorter than those mobilised later. After adjustment for mobility before the fracture, dementia, American Society of Anesthesiologists grade, delirium and postoperative hypotension, the hazard ratio for discharge was 1.03 (95 percent CI 0.97 to 1.10), indicating no clear difference. The authors argue that sicker patients are mobilised later and stay longer for reasons unrelated to mobilisation, and caution that adjusting for delirium and hypotension after surgery may remove part of a real effect.

records.title: Mobilisation within 24 or 48 hours of hip fracture surgery and length of stay: a systematic review of nine studies with meta-analysis of four trials
records.authors: Harrington-Iwu P, Tanaka-Lindholm S, Mbeki-Castro R
records.abstract: We included nine studies of mobilisation within 24 or 48 hours of hip fracture surgery: four randomised trials and five observational studies. In the trials, early mobilisation shortened length of stay (mean difference minus 1.9 days, 95 percent CI minus 3.5 to minus 0.3) with substantial heterogeneity (I squared 64 percent). Observational studies gave inconsistent results, from large reductions to no difference after adjustment. Trials excluded many patients with dementia or delirium, limiting applicability to routine care. The certainty of evidence was rated low.

records.title: Why patients are not mobilised on the day after hip fracture surgery: reasons documented in physiotherapy notes
records.abstract: We read the physiotherapy notes of 310 patients who were not mobilised within 24 hours of hip fracture surgery in three hospitals. Documented reasons were postoperative hypotension in 31 percent, no physiotherapist available at the weekend in 28 percent, delirium or drowsiness in 22 percent, uncontrolled pain in 12 percent and other reasons in 7 percent. Weekend admissions were twice as likely to wait more than 48 hours. The authors note that only the weekend staffing reason is independent of how unwell the patient is.

records.title: Confounding by indication in studies of early mobilisation: a methodological note
records.abstract: Observational comparisons of early and late mobilisation are distorted because the reasons for delay also predict long stays. Postoperative hypotension and delirium both delay mobilisation and predict longer stays, yet they may also be partly caused by immobility, so adjusting for them can remove a real effect while not adjusting leaves confounding. We recommend adjusting for characteristics measured before surgery, reporting estimates with and without postoperative conditions, and using reasons for delay that are unrelated to the patient, such as weekend staffing, as a check on confounding.

records.title: Weekend physiotherapy cover and time to first mobilisation after hip fracture: an interrupted time series
records.abstract: One trauma unit introduced physiotherapy cover on Saturdays and Sundays and compared 18 months before with 18 months after the change. Median time from surgery to first mobilisation fell from 38 to 22 hours, and the proportion mobilised within 24 hours rose from 48 to 71 percent. Mean length of stay fell by 1.1 days, but the confidence interval included no change and a new discharge coordinator started during the same period. The authors conclude that weekend cover reliably speeds mobilisation while its effect on length of stay remains uncertain.

records.title: Measuring time to first mobilisation from clinical notes: agreement between physiotherapy and nursing entries
records.abstract: We compared the time of first mobilisation after hip fracture surgery recorded in physiotherapy entries and in nursing entries for 400 patients. The two sources agreed within two hours for 84 percent of patients. Where they disagreed, the physiotherapy entry usually recorded standing with help while the nursing entry recorded sitting out of bed. Reading one set of paper notes took a median of 22 minutes. We recommend defining first mobilisation as standing or walking with a physiotherapist and using the physiotherapy entry, with the nursing entry as a check.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level, with conflicting evidence. A randomised trial found stays 2.3 days shorter with mobilisation within 24 hours, but it excluded about 30 percent of patients, including those with severe dementia, hypotension or delirium; a national registry found a three-day crude difference that disappeared after adjustment; a review found shorter stays in trials with high heterogeneity and inconsistent observational results. The conflict is about confounding and applicability, recorded as a high-uncertainty inference (c3). Methods guidance favours adjustment for pre-surgical characteristics, with postoperative conditions as a sensitivity analysis and weekend-related delay as a check. Mobilisation time can be read reliably from physiotherapy entries.
response.gradeRationale: Trial evidence of benefit in selected patients conflicts with adjusted routine-care data; heterogeneity and indirectness to patients with dementia or delirium lower certainty. Low certainty that early mobilisation shortens stays in routine care.
response.summary: Seven retrieved records; six claims recorded, one an inference with high uncertainty over conflicting records; overall certainty low.

steps.note: Conflicting evidence is recorded honestly: claim c3 is an inference resting on three retrieved records (trial, registry analysis and review) with uncertainty 'high'. Appraisal on the production scan path requires S13.

response.reading: Early mobilisation sits on a path where the reasons for delay (hypotension, delirium) also lengthen stays, so a crude comparison overstates benefit and heavy adjustment may understate it. Weekend staffing is the one reason for delay that does not depend on the patient, which makes it a useful check. Trial benefit comes from selected patients with seven-day cover; the unit's patients include many the trials left out.

response.designSummary: Case-control study with frequency matching by year and operation type.
response.sampleSize: About 240 notes fit the 100 approved hours at 25 minutes each: 80 cases and 160 controls. If about 55 percent of controls were mobilised within 24 hours, the study has about 82 percent power at two-sided alpha 0.05 to detect an odds ratio of 0.45 and about 71 percent power for 0.50; smaller associations will be estimated imprecisely and reported with their confidence intervals.
response.primaryAnalysis: Unconditional logistic regression of case status on early mobilisation, adjusted for year and operation type (matching factors) and for age, pre-fracture mobility, dementia and American Society of Anesthesiologists grade; about 11 cases per parameter.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Sensitivity analysis adding postoperative hypotension and delirium; the estimate restricted to patients whose delay was due to weekend staffing; the estimate in patients with dementia reported as exploratory; discharge destination by exposure.
response.missingData: Notes without a documented time of first mobilisation are counted and reported; the primary analysis excludes them, with sensitivity analyses coding them first as early and then as late.
response.multiplicity: One primary estimate; sensitivity and subgroup estimates reported with confidence intervals only.
response.software: R; the reading form, the directed acyclic graph and the analysis code archived before reading starts.
overfittingGuards: Adjustment set fixed from a directed acyclic graph before reading
Subgroups limited to weekend delay and dementia

response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: patients with dementia, the oldest patients and those admitted from care homes are least represented in the trial evidence and most affected by long stays; the estimate is reported for patients with dementia, and weekend admissions are examined because they wait longest.
response.effectiveness: The study informs whether weekend physiotherapy cover is worth proposing; a precise null result would redirect effort to other causes of long stays.
response.grants: None needed; a positive result would support a proposal to test weekend cover.

response.discussion: The discussion will set the estimate against the conflicting trial and registry findings and state what it means for weekend physiotherapy cover.
response.limitations: Residual confounding; notes of variable quality; one unit; modest power.
